newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: US seeks right "formula" on WTO infotech deal.
newsitem.headline: US seeks right "formula" on WTO infotech deal.

text.p: U.S. trade officials said on Wednesday they were seeking the right formula for a successful Information Technology Agreement by the conclusion of the first World Trade Organization (WTO) ministerial on Friday.

An official told reporters that a "tremendous amount of work" has been done in the past 48 hours to reach a successful agreement with as many countries as possible and set out a process by which others may join.
"We are continuing to work with our Quad (Canada, European Union, United States and Japan) partners and with many other delegations to find a formula that will succeed," the U.S. trade official said.

He said ministers were considering a proposal that sets out the process by which countries will change their schedules -- lists of products and the tariffs levied on them -- on file at the WTO in Geneva since the end of the 1986-93 Uruguay Round of world trade talks.

The declaration would be adopted by the entire 128 assembled countries at the WTO meeting in Singapore and would be sponsored by those countries who have worked closely on the technology agreement, the official said.
About 9,000 product descriptions -- listing all goods traded around the world by WTO members -- are also on file in Geneva of which ITA items account for about 300, the official said.
In their new ITA schedules, each country involved in the negotiations would have to declare the date it will agree to remove tariffs on them, or reductions they would make to present tariff levels.

The official said an ITA would cover about $500 billion of traded items. The hope is that enough countries will sponsor a declaration at the WTO to spur others to file similar tariff reductions, he said.
"Assuming the ITA were successful at the end of the week, there would be some kind of ministerial declaration that set out the procedure for making the changes in the schedules," the official said.
"It's clear that a large volume of trade is involved and there is an enormous incentive for other countries to come in and file changed schedules on the date," the official said.
